title: NFAs: machines that can guess
summary: Say what 'deterministic' means and the two ways an NFA breaks the DFA rule; run an NFA by hand with processes (copy on a choice, halt on no arrow); decide accept or reject with the h ∧ c ∧ f rule; find L(M) for a small NFA in set-builder form; answer Chen's ten true/false questions.
sourceNote: Lesson 8 slides 'NFA 1: Introduction' (Sep 18, pulled from Canvas); Linz ch. 2.2. Assignment 4 (DFA/NFA quiz, due Sep 29) covers lessons 1 to 8.

blocks.md: **The problem with DFAs** A DFA must have **exactly one** arrow for every symbol out of every state. So even a tiny language like {abb} needs a trap state and a pile of arrows into it, just to say 'no'. The machine also has to read every symbol, even when the answer is already obvious.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: An **NFA** (nondeterministic finite automaton) drops that rule. A state may have **no** arrow for a symbol, or **more than one**. The drawing gets much simpler, and it turns out NFAs recognize exactly the same languages as DFAs (you'll prove that with the subset construction in Lessons 9 and 10).

**Where you'll meet this** Every regex engine (grep, your editor's search, Python's `re`) starts by turning the pattern into an NFA, because that's easy to build from a regex piece by piece. Then it either simulates the NFA directly (exactly what this lesson does) or converts it to a DFA for speed. Lexers in compilers work the same way.

blocks.body: The whole sequence of configurations, from when the machine starts until it halts. If the machine never halts, there is no computation.

M₁ and M₂ are **equivalent** iff **L(M₁) = L(M₂)** over Σ: they accept exactly the same set of strings. Chen's warning: 'two machines are equivalent if both accept a same string' is **wrong**. One shared string is not enough; the whole languages must match.
At every timeframe there is **no more than one** possible transition: 0 or 1. A DFA is the strict special case: **exactly** 1, never 0.
Writing 'equivalent if they accept the same language' is fine; writing 'equivalent if they both accept a string w' is the wrong definition Chen puts on the slide on purpose.

blocks.prompt: A machine has a state with no arrow for 'b'. Is it deterministic?
blocks.answer: Yes, it can still be deterministic: 'no more than one' allows zero. It is just not a DFA (a DFA needs exactly one).

sections.heading: How an NFA runs: the two violations

blocks.md: An NFA is built from the same three blocks as a DFA: an input tape (read only, left to right), a control unit, and a result. It starts the same way. The only new questions are what happens when a DFA rule is broken.

rows: no arrow for the current symbol (violation #1)
**halts**; this process **rejects** because a symbol was not consumed
**copies itself**: one process per arrow, each continues alone
follows it, just like a DFA
blocks.title: Violation #1 and #2

blocks.body: One copy of the machine following one sequence of choices. When there are two possible arrows, the NFA 'replicates the entire structure' and starts a new process with the current configuration; from then on the processes run independently.

blocks.title: The halt, accept and reject rules (Chen's logic)
blocks.body:
h = the process halts
c = all input symbols are consumed
f = it is in an accepting (final) state
a = it accepts

Halts:    (c ∨ z) ⇔ h      z = zero possible transitions
Accepts:  (h ∧ c ∧ f) ⇔ a
Rejects:  (¬h ∨ ¬c ∨ ¬f) ⇔ ¬a     (De Morgan)

The WHOLE NFA accepts if at least one process accepts.
It rejects only if every process rejects.

blocks.md: Why can't you simplify h ∧ c ∧ f? Because in an NFA a process can halt **before** reading everything (h true, c false). In a DFA halting and consuming everything always happen together; here they don't.

blocks.body: Saying 'the NFA is in an accepting state, so it accepts'. Being in an accepting state is only f. You also need the process to have halted with every symbol consumed.

blocks.prompt: A process is in accepting state q₃, but there is still one unread symbol and q₃ has no arrow for it. Accept or reject?
blocks.answer: Reject. It halts (no transition) with a symbol not consumed: c is false, so h ∧ c ∧ f is false.

sections.heading: Example 2: a choice, and two processes

blocks.md: In this machine, q₁ has **two** arrows for **a**: one to q₂, one to q₄. That is violation #2, so reading an a in q₁ splits the machine into two processes.

blocks.caption: Run ba: after 'b' there is one process (in q₁); after 'a' there are two, in q₂ and q₄. q₄ accepts, so ba is accepted. Then click baa and baba in the test set.

frames.caption: Start configuration. Only q₀ is active.

lines: time 1: read b → q1 (one arrow, no split)
frames.caption: q₀ has exactly one arrow for b. Nothing special.

lines: time 2: read a → TWO arrows: q2 and q4
frames.caption: q₁ has two arrows for a: the NFA copies itself. Each copy continues with the rest of the tape (one more a).

lines: process #2: q4 has no arrow for a → halts, 'a' not consumed → REJECT
frames.caption: Process #2 is stuck: q₄ only has an arrow for b. It halts with a symbol left, so it rejects.

lines: process #1: q3, all symbols consumed, q3 accepting → ACCEPT
overall: ACCEPT (at least one process accepts)
frames.caption: One accepting process is enough.

blocks.title: baba: every process rejects (Example 3)
blocks.body:
b → q1
a → split: #1 in q2, #2 in q4
b → #1: q2 has no arrow for b → halts, reject
    #2: q4 -b→ q4
a → #2: q4 has no arrow for a → halts, reject

All processes reject → the NFA rejects baba.

blocks.title: What language is this? (Chen's exercise)

blocks.answer: Yes. b → q₁, a → {q₂, q₄}. The q₂ process dies on b; the q₄ process loops on b and ends in accepting q₄ with everything consumed.

blocks.title: Run this for each process (Lesson 8 appendix)
blocks.body:
1. All symbols consumed?
     yes → in an accepting state? yes: ACCEPT*   no: REJECT**
     no  → go to 2
2. Any transition for (current state, current symbol)?
     no  → REJECT** (halt, symbol not consumed)
     yes → consume one symbol and move
           (more than one arrow? copy the process first)
           then back to 1

* the NFA accepts if ONE process accepts
** the NFA rejects only if ALL processes reject

blocks.md: To get good at this fast, write the **set** of states the processes are in after each symbol: start {q₀}, after b {q₁}, after a {q₂, q₄}, and so on. If the final set contains an accepting state, accept. The sims show this line under the tape. That set-tracking is exactly the subset construction you'll do in Lesson 10.

blocks.title: M₂: one state q, accepting, no arrows

blocks.caption: M₃ from the exercise slide. Before you look at the answer below, test some strings: which ones reach q₂ with nothing left over?

blocks.title: M₃: q₀ loops on a; q₀ -b→ q₁; q₁ loops on b; q₁ -a→ q₂; q₀ -a→ q₂; q₂ loops on a; q₂ accepting
blocks.body:
Route 1: aⁿ, then a into q2, then more a's: all a's, at least one.
Route 2: aⁿ, b, more b's, then a into q2, then more a's.
Both routes: some a's, then some b's (maybe none), then at least one a.

L(M₃) = {aⁿ bᵐ aᵏ : n ≥ 0, m ≥ 0, k ≥ 1}

blocks.prompt: Why is λ NOT in L(M₃)?
blocks.answer: The only accepting state is q₂ and q₀ is not accepting. With no input the machine halts in q₀: all consumed but not accepting.

exercises.title: Run it with processes
exercises.prompt: Using the Example 2 NFA (q₀ -b→ q₁, q₁ -a→ q₂ and q₄, q₂ -a→ q₃, q₄ loops on b; q₃ and q₄ accepting), decide babb and baab. For each, list every process and say why it accepts or rejects.
hints: Write the set of active states after each symbol, starting from {q₀}.
When q₁ reads a, there are two processes. Follow each alone.
A process with no arrow for the next symbol halts and rejects right there.
solution: babb: {q0} →b {q1} →a {q2, q4} →b {q4} (q2 died) →b {q4}. The q4 process consumes everything and q4 accepts: ACCEPT.
baab: {q0} →b {q1} →a {q2, q4} →a {q3} (q4 died: no arrow for a) →b ∅ (q3 has no arrow for b). Every process rejects: REJECT.
exercises.why: This is the exact mechanics of the timed Assignment 4 T/F and short answers, and it is how a regex engine runs a pattern.

exercises.title: Accepting state vs accepted string
exercises.prompt: True or false: 'If an NFA is in an accepting state, the input string is accepted.'
hints: What three things must be true for a process to accept?
h ∧ c ∧ f. Being in an accepting state is only f.
Can a process be in an accepting state with symbols still unread?
solution: False. Acceptance needs h ∧ c ∧ f: halted, all symbols consumed, accepting state. A process can pass through an accepting state mid-string (Example 1: abba reaches q3 with one 'a' left) and still reject.
exercises.why: Chen reuses these T/F statements on quizzes almost word for word.

choices.feedback: Right: it also has to halt with every symbol consumed.
abba reaches accepting q₃ after 'abb' but still has an 'a' to read, and q₃ has no arrow for it: reject.
